---
title: "Semiconductor Manufacturing (SECOM)"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
```

UCI SECOM dataset (`archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/179/secom`): process-control data from a semiconductor wafer fabrication line. **1567 lots**, processed sequentially between 2008-07-19 and 2008-10-17 (irregular spacing — median 37 minutes between lots, occasional multi-day gaps for downtime). Each lot carries **590 sensor channels** recorded during processing (chamber temperatures, pressures, flows, etc. — anonymized, no channel names) plus a pass/fail label.

This is a different kind of candidate than the other real-data chapters: there's no documented change-point event (no antenna log, no dam-closure date, no CO2 protocol). Any mean shift has to be *discovered* by screening the 590 channels, not given. This chapter is exploratory — it screens for candidate sensor pairs before committing to a chapter structure.

```{R secom-load}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

X_raw <- read.table("../data/secom/secom.data", header = FALSE, sep = " ", na.strings = "NA")
labels <- read.table("../data/secom/secom_labels.data", header = FALSE, sep = " ")
names(labels) <- c("label", "time")
labels$time <- as.POSIXct(gsub("\"", "", labels$time), format = "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M:%S")

miss_frac <- colMeans(is.na(X_raw))
var_col <- apply(X_raw, 2, var, na.rm = TRUE)
const_col <- var_col == 0 | is.na(var_col)
good_cols <- which(!const_col & miss_frac < 0.02)

X_good <- X_raw[, good_cols]
X_complete <- X_good[complete.cases(X_good), ]
```

Of 590 channels, `r sum(const_col)` are constant and `r sum(miss_frac > 0.05)` are missing more than 5% of lots — dropping those (and requiring < 2% missingness) leaves **`r length(good_cols)` usable channels**, `r nrow(X_complete)` complete lots.

## Screening for candidates

For each usable channel, a shift score compares the mean of the first third of the run to the last third, scaled by the channel's SD. Among the most-shifted channels, we then look for pairs that are correlated with each other (so there's a real "two series, one relationship" story) but not near-duplicates (correlation close to ±1 usually means two sensors reading the same physical thing).

```{R secom-screen}
#| echo: false

n <- nrow(X_complete)
first_third <- 1:floor(n / 3)
last_third <- (n - floor(n / 3) + 1):n

shift_score <- sapply(X_complete, function(v) abs(mean(v[first_third]) - mean(v[last_third])) / sd(v))
names(shift_score) <- good_cols

C <- cor(X_complete)
colnames(C) <- rownames(C) <- good_cols
```

Three flavors of candidate turned up, none as clean as the other real-data chapters:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Gradual drift

```{R fig-secom-drift}
#| echo: false

cols <- c(170, 305, 441)
df <- X_raw[, cols]
names(df) <- paste0("s", cols)
df$idx <- seq_len(nrow(df))
df <- df[complete.cases(df), ] |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("s"), names_to = "sensor", values_to = "value")

ggplot(df, aes(idx, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~sensor, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Sensors 170, 305, 441 — gradual drift", x = "lot index", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Level creeps up smoothly across the whole three-month run — no dateable event, more like the ozone seasonal drift than a discrete shift. But these three correlate at r = 0.976–0.996 with each other: almost certainly redundant reads of the same physical quantity, not two genuinely different things that happen to move together.

## Saturating sensors

```{R fig-secom-saturating}
#| echo: false

cols <- c(26, 28, 32)
df <- X_raw[, cols]
names(df) <- paste0("s", cols)
df$idx <- seq_len(nrow(df))
df <- df[complete.cases(df), ] |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("s"), names_to = "sensor", values_to = "value")

ggplot(df, aes(idx, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~sensor, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Sensors 26, 28, 32 — saturating / duty-cycle-like", x = "lot index", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Pinned near a ceiling most of the time with sporadic dips to a floor — a bounded or duty-cycle-type signal, not a smoothly-varying mean. Poor fit for ECE's piecewise-constant-mean, fixed-covariance model.

## Discrete step

```{R fig-secom-step}
#| echo: false

cols <- c(544, 545, 546)
df <- X_raw[, cols]
names(df) <- paste0("s", cols)
df$idx <- seq_len(nrow(df))
df <- df[complete.cases(df), ] |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("s"), names_to = "sensor", values_to = "value")

ggplot(df, aes(idx, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~sensor, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Sensors 544, 545, 546 — discrete step near lot 730", x = "lot index", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{R secom-step-detail}
#| echo: false

cols <- c(544, 545, 546)
df <- X_raw[, cols]
names(df) <- paste0("s", cols)
df <- df[complete.cases(df), ]
bp <- 93  # index into complete-case subset where the flat pre-shift segment ends
pre <- df[1:bp, ]
post <- df[(bp + 1):nrow(df), ]
```

The cleanest thing resembling a dateable event: all three jump together around lot 730 (2008-08-04, ~17:46) — plausibly a real recipe, tool, or calibration change. Two caveats keep this from being a clean case: `s544` and `s546` correlate at r = 0.99 (likely redundant), and all three read essentially **zero/constant before the shift** (`r round(sd(pre$s544), 4)`, `r round(sd(pre$s545), 4)`, `r round(sd(pre$s546), 4)` — pre-shift SDs), so "pre-regime correlation" is undefined rather than just biased. That's closer to "sensor was off, then turned on" than "same relationship, obscured by a mean shift."

:::

Of the three, the gradual-drift cluster (`s170`, `s305`, `s441`) is the one we dig into below — despite the near-duplicate correlation, its smoothly-varying mean is the closest match to ECE's model of anything found in this screen, and it follows the same rolling-mean-baseline approach used in `air-pollution.qmd`.

## Diagnostics: Gradual Drift Cluster

```{R secom-drift-load}
#| echo: false
#| label: secom-drift-load

cols <- c(170, 305, 441)
X_data <- X_raw[, cols]
names(X_data) <- c("s170", "s305", "s441")
X_data$idx <- seq_len(nrow(X_data))
X_data <- X_data[complete.cases(X_data[, c("s170", "s305", "s441")]), ]

X_mat <- as.matrix(X_data[, c("s170", "s305", "s441")])
win   <- 25
```

```{R secom-drift-residuals}
#| echo: false
#| label: secom-drift-residuals

X_roll  <- apply(X_mat, 2, rolling_mean, window = win)
colnames(X_roll) <- colnames(X_mat)
X_resid <- X_mat - X_roll
```

```{R secom-drift-tables}
#| echo: false
#| label: secom-drift-tables

ece_cor  <- ece.cor(X_mat) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor) <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

X_resid_complete <- X_resid[complete.cases(X_resid), ]
rolling_cor <- cor(X_resid_complete) |> round(3)
pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

ece_pmat     <- ece_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
rolling_pmat <- cor_pval(X_resid_complete) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{R fig-secom-drift-series}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Sensors 170, 305, 441, faceted. Blue = rolling mean."
#| fig-height: 7

X_long <- X_data |>
  select(idx, s170, s305, s441) |>
  bind_cols(as.data.frame(X_roll) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_roll"), everything())) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -idx, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    type = if_else(str_ends(series, "_roll"), "Rolling Mean", "Raw"),
    sensor = str_remove(series, "_roll$")
  )

ggplot(X_long, aes(x = idx, y = value)) +
  geom_line(data = ~ filter(.x, type == "Raw"), color = "gray50", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = ~ filter(.x, type == "Rolling Mean"), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~sensor, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Sensors 170, 305, 441", x = "lot index", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Residuals

```{R fig-secom-drift-residual}
#| echo: false

X_data |>
  select(idx) |>
  bind_cols(as.data.frame(X_resid)) |>
  pivot_longer(-idx, names_to = "sensor", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(idx, value, color = sensor)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(title = "Rolling-Mean Residuals", x = "lot index", y = "Sensor anomaly", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### ACF

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Naive

```{R acf-secom-drift-naive}
#| echo: false

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1), oma = c(2, 0, 0, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
acf(X_resid[, "s170"], main = "s170", na.action = na.pass)
acf(X_resid[, "s305"], main = "s305", na.action = na.pass)
acf(X_resid[, "s441"], main = "s441", na.action = na.pass)
mtext("Lag (lots)", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.5)
```

Lag-1 residual autocorrelation is essentially zero (-0.06 to -0.07) — unlike ozone's rolling residuals, there's no leftover day-to-day persistence here once the drift is removed. Lot-to-lot readings really do behave close to independent.

#### Mean-Shift-Invariant

```{R acf-secom-drift-invariant}
#| echo: false

plot_sip_acf(X_mat)
```

`SIP::SIP.acf` on the raw series agrees with the naive rolling-residual ACF: near-zero at every lag. With no real autocorrelation to discount, naive and mean-shift-invariant ACF have nothing to disagree about here.

:::

### Correlation

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_cor,     caption = "ECE Correlation")
knitr::kable(rolling_cor, caption = "Rolling Correlation")
knitr::kable(pearson_cor, caption = "Pearson Correlation")
```

Unlike ozone, all three methods land in the same place: **0.97–0.996** across every pair, whichever way the mean is handled. That's consistent with the redundant-sensor read on this cluster from the screening section — if `s170`/`s305`/`s441` are genuinely near-duplicate reads of one physical quantity, there's no mean-shift confound for ECE to correct, because Pearson was never wrong on this cluster to begin with. This cluster doesn't demonstrate ECE's advantage; it demonstrates the boundary case where naive and ECE agree because the naive answer was already right.

### P-Values

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_pmat,     caption = "ECE P-Values")
knitr::kable(rolling_pmat, caption = "Rolling P-Values")
knitr::kable(pearson_pmat, caption = "Pearson P-Values")
```

All three methods reject independence at every pair (p ≈ 0) — no surprise given correlations this high.

:::

## Where this leaves us

The gradual-drift cluster is clean in the sense that matters for diagnostics (near-zero residual autocorrelation, a genuinely smooth mean shift), but it's not a case where naive correlation needed correcting — it's a control case where naive and ECE agree, most likely because the three sensors aren't independent measurements to begin with. The discrete-step and saturating clusters remain open if a genuine naive-vs-ECE divergence (a real "the mean shift fooled Pearson" story) is wanted; so does further screening for a pair that's correlated but not redundant.
